chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, from some of our companions, from Abdullah ibn Kathir, from Abdullah ibn Muskan, who traced it back (marfu'): He said,

The Messenger of God (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever judges in a matter of two dirhams with an unjust ruling and then compels [acceptance of] it would be among the people of this verse:
"and whoever did not judge by what God revealed, those are the disbelievers" [Quran 5:44]

So I said: 'And how does he compel [acceptance of] it?' So he said: 'He would have a whip and a prison, so he judges over it. If [the aggrieved party] accepts his ruling, [well and good]; otherwise he strikes them with his whip and imprisons them in his prison.'

key_terms.جَبَر: Coercion, compelling acceptance by force — the element that transforms a bad ruling into a graver sin
key_terms.جَوْر: Injustice, oppression, deviation from the right path — especially in judicial contexts
key_terms.حُكُومَة: Governance, judicial ruling, the act of adjudication
key_terms.دِرْهَمَيْن: Two dirhams — an intentionally minimal amount, emphasizing there is no threshold below which injustice is excused

ai.seo_question: What did the Prophet say about judges who rule unjustly and compel acceptance of their rulings?
ai.summary: The Prophet (SAWW) links unjust judicial coercion — even in minor monetary disputes of only two dirhams — to the grave Quranic condemnation of those who do not judge by God's revelation (5:44). The narrator then asks the Imam how such compulsion works in practice, and the Imam explains that a corrupt judge enforces his unjust rulings through the physical instruments of state power: the whip and the prison. This hadith is addressed in the context of a discourse on judges who rule by other than divine law, emphasizing that even trivially small cases of unjust adjudication carry enormous spiritual and legal consequences when combined with coercive enforcement.
